A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same ProstaTD study, with matching data sources, annotation definitions and corresponding detection benchmarks. v1 ends with references; v2's Appendices A–I were also inspected.

before.justification: v1 reports original detector evaluations in Tables 4–5, alongside dataset and tracking annotation statistics.

after.justification: v2 reports original cross-validation benchmarks, surgeon agreement measurements, detector ablations and per-class analyses in Tables 3–5 and 8–10.

M1.justification: v1's YOLO-Triplet combines YOLOv12 instrument detection with cropped-region cross-attention and ResNet18-based action/target recognition. v2 replaces this with TDnet's teacher–student architecture, auxiliary component heads, shared positive assignments and instance-level self-distillation using mixed hard/soft targets (Appendix E). This changes architecture and training, beyond renaming.

E1.justification: Detection retains the same 21 prostatectomy videos, three sources and component vocabularies. However, v1 Table 3 includes aspirator–retract–catheter, whereas v2 Table 6 omits it and adds needle-driver–grasp–prostate. This modestly revises represented triplet coverage despite both versions reporting 89 categories; larger frame counts alone do not broaden coverage.

E2.justification: Table 4 adds Faster R-CNN, Cascade R-CNN, SSD, ViT-Det, TAPIR and MCIT-IG, while removing YOLOv5, YOLOv8 and YOLOv9. Table 5 also adds Deformable-DETR, TAPIR and MCIT-IG to the precision/recall comparison, substantially revising comparator membership.

E3.justification: The single 14/2/5-video training/validation/test split becomes five-fold cross-validation over all 21 videos. Dataset totals increase from 60,529 to 71,775 frames and 165,567 to 196,490 instances. v2 also introduces video-wise evaluation and an annotation-review protocol involving five independent surgeons and 1,000 sampled frames.

E4.justification: v2 supplies self-distillation and multitask ablations, video-wise assessment, confusion-matrix and per-class analyses (Appendix F), plus independent annotation agreement and source-specific distribution analyses. v1's tracking comparisons disappear. Although v1 mentions supplementary confusion analysis, that analysis is absent from the supplied PDF.

E5.justification: v1 reports single-split point estimates without evaluation uncertainty. v2 reports means and standard deviations across five folds in Tables 4, 5, 8 and 9, and Cohen's kappa for annotation agreement in Table 3. These introduce substantial statistical reporting; random-seed replication remains unspecified.

E6.justification: Benchmark scores, rankings, speeds and dataset frequencies change extensively. Table 4 replaces YOLO-Triplet's 36.02% triplet mAP50 and 77.4 FPS with TDnet's 36.1±3.4% and 126.6 FPS under changed data, architecture and evaluation, preventing a same-setting improvement claim. v2 adds agreement, ablation and per-class results, while v1's 204/953 tracking-ID counts disappear.

T1.justification: The basic mathematical task definition is retained. Appendix E adds explicit definitions of shared foreground assignment and teacher/student loss objectives, while Appendix D defines video-wise aggregation. These are localized formal additions; neither version provides theorems, proofs or theoretical guarantees.

C1.justification: The contribution shifts from a multi-source dataset supporting detection and tracking toward a fully supervised detection resource comprising annotation tools, an evaluation toolkit, a benchmark and TDnet. v2 adds novelty claims for tailored annotation tools and instance-level distillation, while dropping tracking from its main contributions.

C2.justification: v2 attributes TDnet's gains to reduced class imbalance and cross-task interference, and adds interpretations of action/target confusions. This replaces v1's discussion of YOLO-Triplet's weak relational head and tracking perspectives. Appendix G.2 newly justifies per-frame detection with tracking deferred to future work; the long-tail limitation is largely retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds COCO-format information, preprocessing rules, exact fold assignments, training hyperparameters, annotation-tool JSON schemas and evaluation-toolkit instructions, plus repository README locations. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without proving that all previously unspecified settings changed. Appendix F.1 nevertheless gives conflicting auxiliary classification weights of 0.5 and 0.1.

R1.justification: Research positioning is substantially revised around classification versus fully supervised detection, inaccessible challenge test annotations and limitations of original ESAD/PSI-AVA labels. New detector, metrics, RiT, SurgiTrack and ByteTrack references support the expanded benchmark and tools, while the earlier standalone tracking-literature discussion is removed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contributions, related work and results discussion undergo extensive rewriting. The tracking section disappears, limitations move to Appendix G, and triplet-frequency analysis moves to Appendix B. Dedicated agreement and reproducibility sections and organized appendices substantially restructure the narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds architecture, software, instrument-variation and confusion-matrix figures, together with agreement, fold, ablation and per-class tables; tracking displays are removed. The frequency table is relocated and expanded by source, the precision/recall table is transposed, and benchmark tables gain uncertainty notation and colored rankings.

improvement.justification: Independent surgeon agreement, five-fold variability reporting, targeted ablations and detailed implementation documentation substantially strengthen validation and reproducibility beyond v1's single-split benchmark and descriptive annotation assurance. Tracking coverage is dropped, and v2 introduces reporting problems: Section 6.3 overstates TDnet's component rankings, and Appendix F.1 conflicts on loss weights. These shortcomings limit precision but do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidential support.
